chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: This book is the primary reference for the Rust programming language.

chapters.title: Shebang
chapters.summary: A shebang is an optional line that is typically used in Unix-like systems to specify an interpreter for executing the file.

chapters.title: Macros
chapters.summary: The functionality and syntax of Rust can be extended with custom definitions called macros. They are given names, and invoked through a consistent syntax: some_extension!(...).

chapters.title: Testing attributes
chapters.summary: The following attributes are used for specifying functions for performing tests. Compiling a crate in “test” mode enables building the test functions along with a test harness for executing the tests. Enabling the test mode also enables the test conditional compilation option.

chapters.title: Derive
chapters.summary: The derive attribute invokes one or more derive macros, allowing new items to be automatically generated for data structures. You can create derive macros with procedural macros.

chapters.summary: The following attributes affect compile-time limits.

chapters.title: Type system attributes
chapters.summary: The following attributes are used for changing how a type can be used.

chapters.title: Debugger attributes
chapters.summary: The following attributes are used for enhancing the debugging experience when using third-party debuggers like GDB or WinDbg.

chapters.title: Types
chapters.summary: Every variable, item, and value in a Rust program has a type. The type of a value defines the interpretation of the memory holding it and the operations that may be performed on the value.

chapters.title: Boolean type
chapters.summary: The boolean type or bool is a primitive data type that can take on one of two values, called true and false.

chapters.title: Numeric types
chapters.summary: The unsigned integer types consist of:

chapters.title: Character type
chapters.summary: The char type represents a single Unicode scalar value (i.e., a code point that is not a surrogate).

chapters.title: String slice type
chapters.summary: The string slice (str) type represents a sequence of characters.

chapters.title: Never type
chapters.summary: The never type ! is a type with no values, representing computations that never complete, also known as diverging computations.

chapters.title: Tuple types
chapters.summary: Syntax TupleType → ( ) | ( ( Type , )+ Type? )

chapters.title: Array types
chapters.summary: Syntax ArrayType → [ Type ; Expression ]

chapters.title: Slice types
chapters.summary: Syntax SliceType → [ Type ]

chapters.title: Struct types
chapters.summary: A struct type is a heterogeneous product of other types, called the fields of the type.1

chapters.title: Enumerated types
chapters.summary: An enumerated type is a nominal, heterogeneous disjoint union type, denoted by the name of an enum item. 1

chapters.title: Union types
chapters.summary: A union type is a nominal, heterogeneous C-like union, denoted by the name of a union item.

chapters.title: Function item types
chapters.summary: When referred to, a function item, or the constructor of a tuple-like struct or enum variant, yields a zero-sized value of its function item type.

chapters.title: Closure types
chapters.summary: A closure expression produces a closure value with a unique, anonymous type that cannot be written out. A closure type is approximately equivalent to a struct which contains the captured values. For instance, the following closure:

chapters.title: Pointer types
chapters.summary: All pointers are explicit first-class values. They can be moved or copied, stored into data structs, and returned from functions.

chapters.summary: Syntax BareFunctionType → ForLifetimes? FunctionTypeQualifiers fn ( FunctionParametersMaybeNamedVariadic? ) BareFunctionReturnType?

chapters.summary: Syntax TraitObjectType → Bounds​1 | dyn​2 Bounds?

chapters.summary: Syntax ImplTraitType → impl Bounds?

chapters.title: Type parameters
chapters.summary: Within the body of an item that has type parameter declarations, the names of its type parameters are types:

chapters.title: Inferred type
chapters.summary: Syntax InferredType → _

chapters.title: Dynamically sized types
chapters.summary: Most types have a fixed size that is known at compile time and implement the trait Sized. A type with a size that is known only at run-time is called a dynamically sized type (DST) or, informally, an unsized type. Slices, trait objects, and str are examples of DSTs.

chapters.title: Type layout
chapters.summary: The layout of a type is its size, alignment, and the relative offsets of its fields. For enums, how the discriminant is laid out and interpreted is also part of type layout.

chapters.title: Interior mutability
chapters.summary: Sometimes a type needs to be mutated while having multiple aliases. In Rust this is achieved using a pattern called interior mutability.

chapters.title: Subtyping and variance
chapters.summary: Subtyping is implicit and can occur at any stage in type checking or inference.

chapters.title: Trait and lifetime bounds
chapters.summary: Syntax Bounds → Bound ( + Bound )* +?

chapters.title: Type coercions
chapters.summary: Type coercions are implicit operations that change the type of a value. They happen automatically at specific locations and are highly restricted in what types actually coerce.

chapters.title: Divergence
chapters.summary: A diverging expression is an expression that never completes normal execution.

chapters.title: Destructors
chapters.summary: When an initialized variable or temporary goes out of scope, its destructor is run or it is dropped. Assignment also runs the destructor of its left-hand operand, if it’s initialized. If a variable has been partially initialized, only its initialized fields are dropped.

chapters.title: Lifetime elision
chapters.summary: Rust has rules that allow lifetimes to be elided in various places where the compiler can infer a sensible default choice.

chapters.title: Special types and traits
chapters.summary: Certain types and traits that exist in the standard library are known to the Rust compiler. This chapter documents the special features of these types and traits.

chapters.title: Names
chapters.summary: An entity is a language construct that can be referred to in some way within the source program, usually via a path. Entities include types, items, generic parameters, variable bindings, loop labels, lifetimes, fields, attributes, and lints.

chapters.title: Namespaces
chapters.summary: A namespace is a logical grouping of declared names. Names are segregated into separate namespaces based on the kind of entity the name refers to. Namespaces allow the occurrence of a name in one namespace to not conflict with the same name in another namespace.

chapters.title: Scopes
chapters.summary: A scope is the region of source text where a named entity may be referenced with that name. The following sections provide details on the scoping rules and behavior, which depend on the kind of entity and where it is declared. The process of how names are resolved to entities is described in the name resolution chapter

chapters.title: Preludes
chapters.summary: A prelude is a collection of names that are automatically brought into scope of every module in a crate.

chapters.title: Paths
chapters.summary: A path is a sequence of one or more path segments separated by :: tokens. Paths are used to refer to items, values, types, macros, and attributes.

chapters.title: Name resolution
chapters.summary: Name resolution is the process of tying paths and other identifiers to the declarations of those entities. Names are segregated into different namespaces, allowing entities in different namespaces to share the same name without conflict. Each name is valid within a scope, or a region of source text where that name may

chapters.summary: Syntax Visibility → pub | pub ( crate ) | pub ( self ) | pub ( super ) | pub ( in SimplePath )

chapters.summary: Warning

chapters.title: Memory allocation and lifetime
chapters.summary: The items of a program are those functions, modules, and types that have their value calculated at compile-time and stored uniquely in the memory image of the rust process. Items are neither dynamically allocated nor freed.

chapters.title: Variables
chapters.summary: A variable is a component of a stack frame, either a named function parameter, an anonymous temporary, or a named local variable.

chapters.title: Panic
chapters.summary: Rust provides a mechanism to prevent a function from returning normally, and instead “panic,” which is a response to an error condition that is typically not expected to be recoverable within the context in which the error is encountered.

chapters.title: Inline assembly
chapters.summary: Support for inline assembly is provided via the asm!, naked_asm!, and global_asm! macros. It can be used to embed handwritten assembly in the assembly output generated by the compiler.

chapters.title: Unsafety
chapters.summary: Unsafe operations are those that can potentially violate the memory-safety guarantees of Rust’s static semantics.

chapters.title: Constant evaluation
chapters.summary: Constant evaluation is the process of computing the result of expressions during compilation. Only a subset of all expressions can be evaluated at compile-time.
